slides.notes: Ask students to classify: spam filter, house-price estimate, music playlists grouped by taste, rainfall for tomorrow.

runs.text: Name the task first. It decides the network, the output layer and the error measure.

rows.text: Multilayer perceptron (tansig hidden layer), or RBF network
A grid of neurons; the winner is the cluster
Dynamic network: focused time-delay network, NARX

runs.text: If in doubt, start with a multilayer perceptron with one hidden layer.

slides.title: The workhorse: the multilayer perceptron
slides.notes: Remind them of Unit 3: this is the 1-S-1 function approximator. "Universal approximator" says a solution exists; it does not say training will find it.

runs.text: a² = purelin( W² tansig( W¹ p + b¹ ) + b² )
One hidden layer of sigmoids, one linear output
Each hidden neuron contributes one smooth step. The output adds the steps together.
With enough hidden neurons it can approximate any smooth function.
For classes, replace the linear output with softmax.
It is the standard first choice for fitting and pattern recognition.

slides.title: The other networks, one line each
slides.notes: These were all met in Units 3 and 4. The point today is when to pick each, not how they learn.

runs.text: The other networks, one line each
Hidden neurons respond only near their own centre. Trains fast and stays quiet far from data, but needs many neurons when there are many inputs.
A competitive layer of prototypes, each carrying a class label. Winners are pulled towards examples of their class and pushed from others.
A grid of neurons. Neighbours on the grid learn similar inputs, so the map shows which groups lie close together.
A multilayer network fed with delayed inputs, and for NARX its own past outputs. It has memory, so it can predict.

slides.title: How many layers, how many neurons?
slides.notes: Hagan: start with more neurons than you think you need, and use early stopping or Bayesian regularisation to prevent overfitting.

runs.text: How many layers, how many neurons?
Start with one hidden layer. Add a second only if one cannot reach the accuracy you need. Deep networks are for images, speech and text.
Fixed by the problem: one per value to predict, or one per class.
Not known in advance. It depends on how many bends the true function has. Start generous, then control it with early stopping or regularisation.
More neurons than needed is safe only if you stop training at the right time.

slides.title: Too few, about right, too many
slides.notes: The figures are illustrative. Students can produce the real curve in the Thermistor Bench or Battery Oracle stations by changing the neuron count.

runs.text: Too few, about right, too many
Training error always falls. Test error turns back up
Left: too few neurons. Both errors are high. The network cannot bend enough.
Middle: both errors are low and close together.
Right: training error keeps falling, test error rises. The network is memorising.
Choose the size from the test curve, never from the training curve.

slides.title: Count the weights before you train
slides.notes: Work 3-5-2 on the board with the class: 5(4) + 2(6) = 32.

runs.text: Count the weights before you train
R inputs, S¹ hidden neurons, S² outputs. The "+1" in each bracket is the bias.
Compare the count with your training examples
33 weights against 140 training orders: about four examples per weight. Reasonable.
81 weights against 42 training orders: the network can memorise every order.
Too many weights for the data is the usual cause of overfitting.
Fewer inputs (L35: features, PCA) also means fewer weights.

slides.title: Choosing the output transfer function
slides.notes: Softmax: a_i = exp(n_i) / sum of exp(n_j). Every output depends on all net inputs, which is why they sum to 1.

runs.text: A sigmoid output on a fitting problem cannot reach values outside its range. Use linear.

slides.title: Which inputs deserve a place?
slides.notes: Hagan describes sensitivity analysis as the derivative of the performance with respect to each input element, summed over the data set.

runs.text: List what could physically affect the answer: for delivery time, the hour, distance, rain and the restaurant. Leave out what cannot.
Sensitivity analysis: measure how much the error changes when each input changes. Inputs with almost no effect are candidates to remove.
Drop the weak input, train again and compare the test error. If it does not get worse, the smaller network is the better one.
An input that adds nothing still adds weights, and weights need data.

slides.title: Training in one picture
slides.notes: This is a recap of Unit 3 backpropagation. L37 covers the three choices hidden in this loop: where to start, how to step, when to stop.

runs.text: Feed an input p through the layers to get the output a.
Error e = t − a. Average the squared errors over the data.
Backpropagation gives the slope of the error for every weight.
Move each weight a small step downhill. Repeat.
Batch training uses all examples for each step. Incremental training updates after every example.

slides.title: Watch a boundary bend as the network grows
slides.notes: Three or four straight-ish edges enclose a circle, which is why three to four neurons are enough.

runs.text: Watch a boundary bend as the network grows
Open TensorFlow Playground. Choose the circle data set with one neuron and train: a straight line, a poor result.
Add neurons one at a time up to four. The boundary closes around the circle.
Switch to the spiral. Add a second layer and more neurons. Watch the test loss, not only the training loss.
How many neurons did the circle need, and why about that many? What happened to the test loss when we kept adding?
Thermistor Bench: change the hidden neurons from 1 to 12 and compare the fits.

slides.title: Try it in NeuroScape
slides.notes: The earlier worlds give a quick refresher on RBF, LVQ and SOM if students have forgotten them.

runs.text: Play stage 3 (Design). Try 2, 8 and 20 neurons on 60 records, then on 200.
The bar comparing the number of weights with the number of training orders.
Fit the sensor curve with 1, 3 and 12 hidden neurons.
One neuron gives one bend. Too many gives wiggles between the points.
Revisit the RBF, LVQ and SOM stations for two minutes each.
How each network differs from the multilayer perceptron.

slides.title: Check your understanding
slides.notes: Reproducing the task-network-output table earns most of the marks.

runs.text: How do you choose the network architecture for a given problem? Discuss the type of network, number of layers and neurons, and the output function.
Identify the task: fitting, pattern recognition, clustering or prediction.
Network for each: MLP or RBF; MLP, RBF or LVQ; SOM; time-delay or NARX.
Layers and neurons: one hidden layer first; size set by complexity, controlled by early stopping.
Output function: linear for fitting, softmax or sigmoid for classes.
Input selection by sensitivity analysis; count weights against data.
